sections.heading: C Bitwise Operators
sections.body:
Note: This is a more advanced topic in C. 
If you are new to programming, don't worry if it feels tricky at first - bitwise operators are mainly used in special cases like system programming, hardware control, or performance optimizations.

In C, bitwise operators let you work directly with the bits (the 1s and 0s) that make up numbers in binary form.

Every integer in a computer is stored in binary, which means it is represented using bits (binary digits) that are either 0 or 1. 
Bitwise operators allow you to compare, combine, shift, or flip these bits.

Note: Bitwise operations only work on integer types (such as int, char, or long).

Tip: If you are not yet familiar with binary numbers, check out these pages first:

- Intro to Programming - Binary Numbers
- Intro to Programming - Bits and Bytes

sections.heading: List of Bitwise Operators
sections.body:
Operator | Name | Description
& | AND | Sets each bit to 1 if both bits are 1
| | OR | Sets each bit to 1 if at least one of the bits is 1
^ | XOR | Sets each bit to 1 if only one of the bits is 1
~ | NOT | Inverts all the bits
<< | Left Shift | Shifts bits to the left (multiplies by powers of 2)
>> | Right Shift | Shifts bits to the right (divides by powers of 2)

sections.heading: Binary Example
sections.body:
Let's start with two integers:

Here's how different bitwise operators work on these values:

Operation | Binary Result | Decimal Result
a & b | 0010 | 2
a | b | 0111 | 7
a ^ b | 0101 | 5
~a | ...1001 | -7 (on most systems)
a << 1 | 1100 | 12
a >> 1 | 0011 | 3
sections.code:
int a = 6;  // 0110 in binary
int b = 3;  // 0011 in binary

sections.heading: Bitwise AND (&)
sections.body: The & operator compares each bit and returns 1 only if both bits are 1.
sections.code:
int a = 6;   // 0110
int b = 3;   // 0011

int result = a & b;
printf("Result: %d\n", result); // 2 (0010)

sections.heading: Bitwise OR (|)
sections.body: The | operator sets a bit to 1 if either bit is 1.
sections.code:
int a = 6;   // 0110
int b = 3;   // 0011

int result = a | b;
printf("Result: %d\n", result); // 7 (0111)

sections.heading: Bitwise XOR (^)
sections.body: The ^ operator returns 1 only when the bits are different.
sections.code:
int a = 6;   // 0110
int b = 3;   // 0011

int result = a ^ b;
printf("Result: %d\n", result); // 5 (0101)

sections.heading: Bitwise NOT (~)
sections.body:
The ~ operator inverts each bit (0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0).

Note: The result of ~ depends on how negative numbers are stored (usually two's complement). For example, 5 (00000101) becomes 11111010, which is interpreted as -6.

sections.heading: Left Shift (<<)
sections.body: The << operator shifts bits to the left and fills in 0s on the right. This is the same as multiplying by powers of 2.

sections.heading: Right Shift (>>)
sections.body: The >> operator shifts bits to the right. This is the same as dividing by powers of 2. On signed integers, the sign bit may be preserved depending on the system.

sections.heading: Real-Life Example: Flags and Permissions
sections.body:
Bitwise operators are often used to store multiple options in a single integer, using flags.

In this example, the user has both READ and WRITE permissions, but not EXEC.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- Bitwise operators work on individual bits of integers
- &: AND - both bits must be 1
- |: OR - either bit can be 1
- ^: XOR - only one bit is 1
- ~: NOT - flips all bits
- <<: Left shift - multiplies by powers of 2
- >>: Right shift - divides by powers of 2

Tip: Bitwise operations are useful for optimization, low-level hardware access, flags, and masks.
